# Lessons of glibc-crustify

Rules that hold for this campaign alone, as `evolution`'s Lessons section describes. Every
run reads them before its first step.

## A batch's gates run with no build variant

**Rule.** libc is the system's, so `build.json` has no variants, and this tree has no
`cargo-variant` script. A batch runs its gates directly, each build in a target dir of its
own under `crustify/tmp/`:

- campaign mode: `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=<plain | asan-ubsan | tsan>` set on every
  `cargo` command that builds the tests, which then regenerate the bindings and check them
  against the committed ones;
- format: `cargo +<the workspace's nightly> fmt --all -- --check`, since `rustfmt.toml`
  uses nightly-only options;
- ASan: on that nightly, `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, with
  `RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"`, and the same flags in
  `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, without which the doctests fail to link against the ASan runtime; TSan:
  the same with `-Zsanitizer=thread` and `-Zbuild-std`. They instrument the Rust alone,
  since the system's glibc is not instrumented, so TSan sees no race inside glibc. The host
  has no `llvm-symbolizer` on its `PATH`, so a sanitizer trace a report carries is
  symbolized with `ASAN_OPTIONS=external_symbolizer_path=/usr/bin/addr2line`;
- coverage: Rust only, measured as the parent's `crustify/scripts/coverage/baseline.sh`
  does, over a scratch copy without `c/`. Its `report.py` rejects the scope, since
  `llvm-cov` prints this tree's file names relative to `src/`, so the `TOTAL` line is read
  from `llvm-cov report` itself. The compile-fail suite fails in the marked copy, which
  only a nightly builds, and it covers nothing.
- a wave's and a module's end gates: `testing-gates`' `end-gates`, with `--stages
  plain,asan-ubsan,tsan,miri` and with `--runner` set to a script in `crustify/tmp/`. Given
  `<variant> <cargo args>`, the script runs `cargo` with the flags above, adding
  `--target-dir` under the worktree's `crustify/tmp/` so that every snapshot reuses one
  build per variant. Miri takes `--stage-env miri:CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=plain` and
  `--stage-env miri:CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<worktree>/crustify/tmp/target-miri`.

**Evidence.** wave-2/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/genops.c`) worked these out by hand.
wave-2/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, wrote the `end-gates` runner by hand too.
wave-3/batch-0/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`) found that the `struct_tm_h` doctest fails to
link under ASan without `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, and passes with it.
wave-4/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/stdio.c`) found the doctests failing to link under ASan with
`RUSTFLAGS` alone (`undefined symbol: __asan_init`), and passing with `RUSTDOCFLAGS`.
wave-4/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, found its reproducer's ASan trace printed as bare
addresses, and symbolized through `addr2line`.

**Scope.** Every batch until the tree gets a variant script.

## A threaded stream test writes a file stream, not an `open_memstream` one

**Rule.** A test that writes one stream from several threads, to check that its writes
hold the stream's lock, opens a file stream (`fopen`), whose buffer glibc allocates once.
An `open_memstream` stream grows its buffer with `malloc` and `free` inside each write,
under the stream's lock. TSan intercepts those calls but not glibc's lock, which is an
uninstrumented futex, so it reports every two threads' reallocations as a data race in
`free` (`_IO_str_overflow`), and the suite fails under TSan though the writes are
serialized. A test with one writing thread may use either.

**Evidence.** wave-3/batch-0/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`):
`writes_from_threads_never_interleave` over `open_memstream` was reported under TSan, and was
clean over `fopen` in five runs. It still fails without the binding's `flockfile`, with
interleaved lines over `fopen` and a glibc abort over `open_memstream`.

**Scope.** Every TSan run over tests that share a C stream between threads, `stderr`'s
(wave 4) included.

## An operation that takes a stream's lock refuses a stream without one

**Rule.** An operation bound on `FileRef` that takes the stream's lock with `flockfile`, or
tries it with `ftrylockfile`, first checks that the stream has a lock (`_lock` non-null), as
`FileRef::print`'s `has_lock` does (`src/libc/stdio_common/fprintf.rs`). If it has none,
the operation returns `io::ErrorKind::Unsupported`, writes nothing and leaves `errno` alone.
glibc's lock routines dereference `_lock` without checking it. glibc's own stdio routines
skip the lock on such a stream, and Rust cannot do the same without breaking `FileRef`'s
`Sync`. Every stream a program opens has a lock, as do the standard streams. The stream
glibc hands the handler of a `register_printf_specifier` conversion has none, and it
honours `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract.

**Evidence.** wave-3/batch-1/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`'s module pass): finding
`contracts/ffi_import/print-locks-a-stream-without-a-lock`, whose reproducer dies with a
SEGV in `flockfile` under ASan on `53dd776`. The unit test
`a_stream_without_a_lock_is_refused` uses the `in_printf_handler` fixture
(`tests/fixtures/stream_unit.rs`), which gives later operations that stream to test against.

**Scope.** Every later operation on `FileRef` that locks the stream, `stderr`'s (wave 4)
included, as long as `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract admits every open stream.

## A test of a failing stream reads what it holds only after its last write

**Rule.** The stream fixture's `contents()` flushes the stream with `fflush` before it reads
it. On a stream whose writes fail, `/dev/full` or full `fmemopen` storage, that flush fails
too: it sets the stream's error indicator and discards its buffer. A test that reads
`contents()` between two writes therefore changes what the second write meets, whether it
fails and whether its failure shows in the indicator. Such a test reads `contents()` once,
after its last write, as `tests/equiv_pub/iofwrite.rs`' `compare_flushing` does with
`Flush::AtEnd`. A stream whose writes succeed may be read after each write.

**Evidence.** wave-5/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/iofwrite.c`):
`a_failed_line_buffered_flush_fails_as_fprintf_does`, read after each write, failed at its
second write. The flush after `"status: "` had set the indicator, which hid the failure of
the `"failed\n"` that followed. Read after the last write, it passes, and it fails when the
binding ignores the indicator.

**Scope.** Every test that writes a failing stream through the fixture, any later stream
operation's, such as `fputs`' or `fflush`'s, included.

name: testing-gates
description: "The regression gates work lands through, by event: a batch's scoped gates, a wave's, a module's end or switch from C and a ship point's; campaign mode and packaging, sanitizers, BSan and Miri, rebases under the landing lock, and a port batch's export checks. Read before running a batch's gates, landing, integrating a module or shipping."
---

# Testing gates

The gates every landing passes, over the tests [`testing`](../SKILL.md) classifies and the
builds [`testing-builds`](../builds/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Regressions

Every batch checks, formats and lints the workspace on the tree it lands, with warnings
denied, as [`toolchain`](../../../rust/toolchain/SKILL.md) describes, and tests what its
change can affect: its module and the modules that depend on it, as `modules.json` records
them, each by its tests' module paths.

Every build of those gates runs in the raw bindings' campaign mode, as
[`bindgen`](../../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Build modes section describes, so that each fails when the
committed bindings do not match their input. A batch that changed the raw bindings, or a
landing that changes `c/`, also packages the safe crate, built alone in bundled mode from
the C it packages, with no build variant selected. Until the out-of-tree wrappers are
published, each crate the package depends on is patched to its local source, so that the
package builds alone.

The tests run against the matching variant, or a private replacement, and each event runs
them to its own depth:

- a batch: the tests above, plain and under ASan/UBSan, and its own tests under each other
  sanitizer its items call for, such as TSan where it asserts `Send` or `Sync` or adds a
  threaded callback, or MSan where C leaves memory it hands over partly unwritten;
- a wave's end: the workspace's tests, and the Miri gate below;
- a module's end, its switch in a port: every test under every available sanitizer,
  and BSan as below; and
- a ship point: every gate over the whole workspace under every available sanitizer, with
  the coverage measurement.
<!-- TODO: a wave's end and a module's end are run by the wave's last review batch and the
module pass, so a campaign without review runs neither: they need an owner there. -->

BSan, when available, is run for every batch and at module end:

- For a batch, it runs only on the individual tests or reproducers the batch expects to
  trigger it, each by exact name and alone; never on a whole test binary, a suite or the
  workspace.
- At module end, it runs as a gate over everything the module landed: the
  whole workspace, one invocation per test binary, as many side by side as
  [`concurrency`](../../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, each under a `timeout`.

A batch runs the tests it wrote under Miri. Miri is also run after every wave, as a gate
over the whole workspace: one Miri run on the pinned nightly per test binary, the library's
and each integration suite's, as many side by side as
[`concurrency`](../../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, each skipping the
compile-fail tests. The gate passes only
with no Miri error: a test that stops at the foreign boundary without the attribute gets
it, and any other Miri error is a UB candidate of the item it touches.

`end-gates`, beside this skill and documented by its `--help`, runs a wave's and a
module's end gates so, over a snapshot of the tree, so that work goes on in the tree while
they run: the workspace under each variant, Miri and BSan per test binary, and the BSan
tests known never to finish skipped by name, each skip checked against its binary's test
list before anything runs.

Each gate run starts in the background and is waited on to exit; its output is neither
polled nor read while it runs. BSan reports false positives at the foreign boundary, so
only a true positive, a report that reproduces through the Rust side as a single test or
standalone reproducer, becomes a UB finding.

Every translation and review batch measures the consumer-facing API of its items against
the tip it rebased onto, each change classified as the dashboard's API stability columns
name them. An item's API is fixed by its first landing: a later landing
that changes or removes it, a port, a later stage, a rebind or a review fix alike, breaks
its consumers, and is kept only with its reason recorded in the batch's notes, such as a
soundness fix; the measure does not fail the gate. A module's integration measures every
item of the module against the module's base, and a ship point the whole crate against the
previous ship point.

When C changed, the configured C build and baseline run. A wrap-only batch with no C
change does not need the full C baseline.

A batch validates its own change on its own base first. Its rebase onto the integration
branch, under the landing lock that [`versioning`](../../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Landing section
describes, then combines that change with the work landed since: the gates run again are
those that could catch a regression the combination introduces, judged from what the
batch's change and the rebased-in changes touch and how they could interact. A gate that
neither side's changes could affect keeps the result it had, and a rebase that conflicts
makes the resolved tree new work of the batch's own.

A `port` batch changes no C: its gates are those above, run against the variants with its
module's export feature off, so that the ported Rust is tested beside the C it replaces.
It also checks and lints the safe crate with that feature on, which compiles the module's
gateway without linking it, and each export is checked at compile time against the raw
binding of the C declaration it replaces, so that a signature that drifts from C's fails
to build.

A module's switch removes its translation unit, and the C tests tied to it that reach
its internals, from `c/`, rebuilds the variants from the C that remains and deletes the
module's export feature, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section
describes. Its gates are a module's end's, in campaign mode over the rebuilt variants, and
the target's remaining C tests, which link the remaining C and the safe crate's Rust static
library, so that the C reaches the ported module through its exports: the module's tied C
tests that use only its public API among them, as the porting workflow's Tests follow
their modules section describes. Before a tied C test leaves, the cases none of the
module's `unit_pub` tests carries over are listed, as [`testing`](../SKILL.md)'s C tests
carried over section describes.

# Campaign layout

Where a campaign's files sit: the repository's tree, its artifact dirs, Crustify's home
and the campaign's scratch and reviews dirs. The repositories, branches and worktrees
that hold them are [`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md)'s.

A repository holds one campaign, and its work is cumulative: a later run resumes it and
skips what it already completed. Its artifact and reviews dirs are grouped by module, and
named from a batch's coordinates in `crustify/artifacts/schedule.json`, its module, wave
index and batch index, and a run's attempt. Nothing records a path; each name below is
spelled from those coordinates.

## 1. Tree

A translation campaign's repository, as [`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories
section names it, is laid out as:

```text
<repository>/
├── Cargo.toml          the safe crate, and the workspace
├── src/                the safe crate's modules, as the conventions lay them out
├── tests/              the safe crate's integration test suites
├── sys/                the raw bindings' generator input and generated bindings, one dir per link unit
├── c/                  the C codebase, the C root, which the safe crate bundles
└── crustify/           the campaign: its settings, artifacts and analysis state
```

The wrappers of the libraries it uses from outside its tree are repositories of their
own, cloned beside it as `../<source>-crustify`, as [`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)
describes.

Every path into the C that the plan records, in `modules.json`, `schedule.json`, the
tools' configurations and tables and a batch item's `defined_in`, is relative to the C
root, `c/`, so that the plan reads as the C codebase lays itself out. Every other path is
relative to the repository's root.

## 2. Ids

A batch's id is the part of its branch name after `crustify/batches/`:
`wave-<index>/batch-<index>`. It is permanent, since a started wave's index is never
reused or renumbered (see `schedule-schema`), and its entry in `schedule.json` gives the batch's link
unit, module, kind and worklist. A run's id is its batch's id followed by its attempt,
numbered from 1 in the order the batch's runs launch: `wave-3/batch-1/run-2`. A planner
run's is `planner/run-<n>`, numbered among the planner runs, which also names its branch.

A module's dir is its branch's name after `crustify/`: `modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or
`foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module. A wave that belongs to no
module, such as an audit's, has `waves` in its place.

## 3. Artifact dirs

The campaign's artifacts sit under `crustify/artifacts/`, with one dir per agent run:

```text
crustify/artifacts/                             the campaign
├── build.json                                  the prebuilt variants of the target
├── modules.json                                the module decomposition
├── dependencies.json                           the out-of-tree libraries the target uses
├── schedule.json                               the waves and batches, and their progress
├── dashboard.md                                the campaign dashboard; audit-dashboard.md for an audit
├── planner/run-<n>/                            a planner run
├── evolution/<slug>/review-<n>/                a review of a change to Crustify or a tool
└── <module dir>/wave-<index>/                  a wave's dir: its own records, such as its scans
    └── batch-<index>/run-<n>/                  a run of a batch, a binder's, a translator's or a reviewer's
        ├── task.json                           its input, with the batch and run fields, and its session id
        ├── task.md                             its task message
        └── …                                   the records its run keeps, as the tool skills name them
```

A batch that is run again gets a new run dir, and every attempt keeps its records. A run's
`task.json` names its batch too. The run dir holds
what the campaign keeps of the run: its input, with the backend, billing, model proxy and
arguments it ran under and the session it became, and the artifacts its agent produced.
Its transcript and pricing record are in crustify's home.

The settings each module or wave ran under are not copied anywhere: they are
`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` as committed at its base, in the working branch's history.

## 4. Lifecycle

A run's dir, with its `task.json`, is created before its agent launches, and kept: every
attempt keeps its records. The campaign's artifact dir is created during setup, with the
working branch.

## 5. Crustify's home

Crustify keeps what belongs to its user rather than to a campaign in its home,
`$CRUSTIFY_HOME` or `~/.crustify`:

```text
~/.crustify/
├── providers/<backend>/              a CLI's config home under API-key billing
├── sessions/<session id>/
│   └── usage.session.json            how a session was priced: its backend, model proxy and rate snapshot
├── rates/<timestamp>.json            the rates `crustify-usage` fetched, kept whenever they changed
└── transcripts/<session id>.jsonl    the agents' transcripts, copied from the CLIs' homes
```

A session's directory is named by its CLI's session id, which its run's `task.json`
records, or, for an agent its host runs inside another session, by the agent's id.

## 6. Scratch

`crustify/tmp/` is gitignored and holds anything residual that is no artifact: downloads,
scratch builds and experiments, intermediate outputs. Residual files go nowhere else in the
repository. An agent's scratch is its own: its worktree's `crustify/tmp/`, never a
directory the host hands every agent of a session, such as a scratchpad its subagents
share, where another agent's run can overwrite it.

## 7. Reviews

A review batch's findings sit under its reviews dir, `crustify/reviews/<module dir>/<batch id>/`,
such as `crustify/reviews/modules/libgit2/src/libgit2/refs.c/wave-3/batch-1/`, in the repository the review lands in, and a planner
run's plan corrections under `crustify/reviews/planner/`, as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Reports and Plan corrections sections
lay them out.

## 8. Evolution

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, and its proposals for Crustify and its
tools under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)
describes.

A run's dir, with its `task.json`, is created before its agent launches, and kept: every
attempt keeps its records. The campaign's artifact dir is created during setup, with the
working branch.

## 5. Crustify's home

Crustify keeps what belongs to its user rather than to a campaign in its home,
`$CRUSTIFY_HOME` or `~/.crustify`:

```text
~/.crustify/
├── providers/<backend>/              a CLI's config home under API-key billing
├── sessions/<session id>/
│   └── usage.session.json            how a session was priced: its backend, model proxy and rate snapshot
├── rates/<timestamp>.json            the rates `crustify-usage` fetched, kept whenever they changed
└── transcripts/<session id>.jsonl    the agents' transcripts, copied from the CLIs' homes
```

A session's directory is named by its CLI's session id, which its run's `task.json`
records, or, for an agent its host runs inside another session, by the agent's id.

## 6. Scratch

`crustify/tmp/` is gitignored and holds anything residual that is no artifact: downloads,
scratch builds and experiments, intermediate outputs. Residual files go nowhere else in the
repository. An agent's scratch is its own: its worktree's `crustify/tmp/`, never a
directory the host hands every agent of a session, such as a scratchpad its subagents
share, where another agent's run can overwrite it.

## 7. Reviews

A review batch's findings sit under its reviews dir, `crustify/reviews/<module dir>/<batch id>/`,
such as `crustify/reviews/modules/libgit2/src/libgit2/refs.c/wave-3/batch-1/`, in the repository the review lands in, and a planner
run's plan corrections under `crustify/reviews/planner/`, as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Reports and Plan corrections sections
lay them out.

## 8. Evolution

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, and its proposals for Crustify and its
tools under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)
describes.

# Versioning

branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a

in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

name: reviewing
description: "How landed work is reviewed: tiered review batches and module passes, depth by how long code lasts, worklists, objectives, reports, reproducers, fixes, gates and plan corrections. Read before reviewing a batch, filing a finding or correcting an earlier plan."
---

# Reviewing

Review inspects work that has already landed, for a set of objectives, and files a report
for every defect it finds. In a translation campaign, it inspects what each
translation batch landed before the waves that build on it start; in an audit, the modules of a crate
that Crustify did not generate (see [`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)); and planner runs review the
plan that earlier runs committed (see [Plan corrections](#9-plan-corrections)).

## 1. Review batches

When review is enabled, every translation batch's landing is reviewed before its wave is
promoted, so that no wave builds on unreviewed work. A review batch is a batch of the wave
it reviews, in `schedule.json`, that `reviews` some of its landed translation batches, and
lands on the same integration branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)
names it. The wave is promoted
once its translation batches and their reviews have landed. An audit's review waves are
[`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)'s.

Review is tiered. Each landing is reviewed within its wave, to the depth
[Depth](#11-depth) gives it. Before a module's switch in a port, and at its end in a
wrap, a module pass reviews the module whole, across its batches: its unsafe regions, its
exports and its tests. It is the last review batch of the last wave of the module's `wrap`
and `port` items, not of a port's later stages, marked
`module_pass`, launched once every other batch of that wave has landed; its worklist is
the module's paths, and it runs the wave's gates and the module's end gates, as
[Gates](#7-gates) describes. A module whose run landed a single translation batch is
reviewed by its module pass alone, whose workset is that batch's whole: a review of the
batch before it would read the same code twice.

Review batches are packed eagerly, as the batches they review land: one launches as soon as
the landed batches not yet reviewed fill it, and the last once every translation batch of
the wave has landed, so that review runs beside the wave's remaining batches rather than
after them. When a session runs only part of a wave, or part of the scope, its review
covers what it landed, before what consumes that starts.

A review batch takes the commits of translation batches of one route, `type` or `symbol`,
counted over their items: types and symbols are reviewed apart. It is larger than a
translation batch, since its reviewer reads landed code rather than writing it, and is
sized as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Batches section sizes one,
from what landed rather than what is planned: its lines, its unsafe sites and raw-pointer
positions, the regions it touches and the objectives it carries, without overwhelming its
reviewer, and within the settings' review caps (`id: review-workload`) when they set them.
A campaign may also review every translation batch on its own, with that batch's commits.

A review batch's `task.json` holds its worklist, its objectives, its wave branch and its
run fields, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Review batches section
describes. Without `objectives`, a batch runs every objective that applies: those this skill's
Objectives section and the tool skills describe.

### 1.1 Depth

How deeply a landing is reviewed follows how long its code lasts, as
[`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s thoroughness does. A wrapper a port will replace, its
item's port planned in `schedule.json`, keeps its safe API through that port: it is
reviewed on its public API, for every objective that applies there, `ergonomics` included,
and not on its internals. An export is reviewed lightly while the C that calls it is
scheduled for porting, and thoroughly once it serves C that stays, for good or when a ship
point releases its module. Everything else is reviewed for every objective that applies.

## 2. Worklists

A review batch has one route:

| route | worklist | workset |
|---|---|---|
| `commits` | commits that translation batches landed | the code they add or change, and what it reaches |
| `paths` | source files and directories of a crate, or named types, trait impls and functions in one | everything they define, or the named parts |
| `reports` | none: the batch only revisits reports | the code the reports name |

A review batch's entry in `schedule.json` names the batches of its wave it
`reviews`, and each of those lists the `commits` it landed and the `items` it bound or
ported, whose `kind` gives their routes, `type` or `symbol`, as
[`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.

A module named with `types`, `trait_impls` or `functions` limits the workset to those: a
type with its fields and its inherent impls, wherever they are; a trait impl, named
`<trait> for <type>` as its header spells it, with its methods and associated items; a
free function with nothing else. What they call and what implements their traits is read,
but only the workset is reported on.

## 3. Objectives

Each objective names a kind of defect. A tool may contribute objectives of its own.

### 3.1 Unsafety (`unsafety`)

Unsafe annotations and raw pointers on the workset's public API that safe, idiomatic
variants could replace, so that API consumers write less unsafe code.

### 3.2 Contracts (`contracts`)

Safety contracts that are incorrect, incomplete or ambiguous:

- the `# Safety` obligation of a public entry point that must legitimately stay unsafe: a
  caller who honours it can still reach undefined behaviour, or it asks for something the
  implementation does not need;
- the `// SAFETY:` justification of an `unsafe` block: the invariant it claims does not
  hold on every path that reaches the block, or no comment justifies the block at all;
- an obligation stated on code that C calls once a value is handed to it, such as the
  members of a callback table a safe constructor builds for C to install: C, not the Rust
  caller, then chooses the arguments, often from data it reads, so no caller can honour it.
  What the obligation excludes is refused in Rust, in front of the C, instead, where Rust
  can test it, such as a value, a range, a null or a length. One Rust cannot test, such as
  a pointer's liveness or family, or a string's terminator, is kept by whoever hands the
  value to C: the C declaration's own contract, which the code it calls trusts as an
  export does, or an `unsafe` installer whose Rust caller vouches for it. Only an
  obligation neither covers, and Rust can test, is a finding.

A contract is tested by trying to break it: an input, a call sequence or an interleaving
that honours the obligation, or reaches the block through safe code, and still violates
what the `unsafe` relies on. Contracts are judged by the side of the boundary they serve:
the gateways through which C reaches the crate, its `ffi_export` regions, and every other
unsafe code, which in a Crustify-generated crate sits in its `ffi_import` regions, whose
items are sound for every input their module can give them, as
[`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section requires.

### 3.3 UB (`ub`)

UB in the workset's API that its UB tests missed, by where it is reached from: the safe
public API, the unsafe public API within its `# Safety` obligations, or C through an
export within the C declaration's contract. The unsafe surface includes only the API the
workset adds; a workset that made no API item unsafe has none.

### 3.4 Equivalence (`equiv`)

Functional equivalence defects in the workset's API that its equivalence tests missed,
while the C it translates exists: in a port, until the module's switch. A divergence is a defect only when it is unintended: a doc comment, a `CHANGELOG`
entry, a named test asserting the new behaviour or a commit message explaining it marks it
deliberate, and one that corrects a C defect on purpose is no finding.

### 3.5 Logic (`logic`)

Behaviour that departs from the library's intended specification, in the workset's public
API or its private implementation, that its tests missed. The specification is, from the
most authoritative: the formats and standards the library implements, its documentation,
what its own test suites assert, and its maintainers' stated intent. A finding cites what
the behaviour departs from. Where the C departs from it too, the defect is not copied into
the Rust, and the finding records the C's. A leak, a deadlock or a panic on valid input
departs from nearly every specification.

### 3.6 Ergonomics (`ergonomics`)

Public API that is harder to use than it needs to be: its names, its conversions, its
iterators, builders or defaults where the C takes long argument lists, and the standard
traits its types lack. An item's safe API is fixed by the first batch that gives it one, a
wrap included, so its ergonomics are reviewed there.

### 3.7 Idiom (`idiom`)

Ported implementation that transliterates its C rather than using Rust's own means: index
loops where iterators fit, status codes where `Result` and `?` fit, lengths and releases
carried by hand where ownership carries them.

### 3.8 Conventions (`conventions`)

Deviations from the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md), in a Crustify-generated
batch only, unsafe code outside its regions included.

### 3.9 Misc (`misc`)

Any other defect in the workset.

### 3.10 Test adequacy (`test-adequacy`)

Gaps in the workset's tests: the C and Rust execution paths, and the states and
transitions, that the codebase's external and inline test suites leave unreached, found by
reading those suites against the code and measured as
[`testing-builds`](../testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section describes; assertions too
weak to fail when the code is wrong; tests outside the suite of their kind; and the C test
cases none carries over. A gap is filled with tests, not filed: the coverage measurement
shows the delta.

### 3.11 Revisit (`revisit`)

The reports an earlier review filed, each rerun through its reproducer on the current
tree. One that still reproduces stays a finding of its objective; one that no longer does
has its report updated with the commit that changed the verdict; one that was never a
defect is removed, with the reason in the commit message.

### 3.12 Disclosure (`disclose`)

A `disclosure.md` beside each report that the user can send to the affected project's
maintainers unchanged: under 450 words, following the project's conventions for
disclosing security and UB issues, in an email-friendly format naming the maintainers when
it goes by email first. It includes a small snippet and the sanitizer crash or failing
assertion, offers the reproducer on request, and offers patches only under `fix`. It ends
with: `Found by [Crustify](https://github.com/crustify-rs/crustify), an experimental
UB/soundness auditing agent developed at UC Berkeley and running on <model name>, then
manually reviewed and independently reproduced.`

### 3.13 Fix (`fix`)

Whether a review patches what it finds. Without it, a review changes nothing outside
its reviews dir but the tests that fill the gaps `test-adequacy` finds.

## 4. Reports

A review batch files its findings under its reviews dir, as
[`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Reviews section spells it,
each in its own `<slug>` directory, holding its report and, when it has one, its
reproducer, in the sub-directory of its objective:

| objective | sub-directory |
|---|---|
| `unsafety` | `unsafe/` |
| `contracts`, of a gateway | `contracts/ffi_export/` |
| `contracts`, of other unsafe code | `contracts/ffi_import/` |
| `ub`, on the safe interface | `ub_safe/` |
| `ub`, on the unsafe interface | `ub_unsafe/` |
| `ub`, through an export | `ub_export/` |
| `equiv` | `equiv/` |
| `logic` | `logic/` |
| `ergonomics` | `ergonomics/` |
| `idiom` | `idiom/` |
| `conventions` | `conventions/` |
| `misc` | `misc/` |

A tool may add sub-directories for findings on its own output. A defect in a tool
rather than in the reviewed codebase, Crustify included, is no finding: it is a proposal,
with its reproducer, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Proposals
section describes.

A report states what is wrong, where, the evidence that proves it, and, under `fix`, how
it was fixed. It carries everything needed to rerun its reproducer from a clean checkout:
the exact command and the sanitizer output or failing assertion it produced. Neither a
report nor a reproducer carries an API key, in a core dump or anywhere else: a reviews dir
may be published.

## 5. Reproducers

A `ub`, `equiv` or `logic` candidate becomes a finding only once a reproducer proves it,
and so does a `contracts` candidate that claims a contract can be broken. A contract that merely
asks for more than the implementation needs, or a missing justification, is a finding
without one.

- A UB reproducer triggers one of the available sanitizers from Rust, and its report
  carries the sanitizer's trace. One targeting the safe public API carries
  `#[forbid(unsafe_code)]`; one targeting the unsafe API, or breaking a contract, honours
  the `# Safety` obligation. One reaching an export calls it as C would, through its raw
  binding, within the C declaration's contract.
- An equivalence reproducer fails one of [`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s equivalence
  comparisons while running the raw C and the public Rust API, and its report carries the
  failing assertion. Once the C is gone, a behaviour finding is a `logic` one.
- A logic reproducer fails a Rust assertion of what the specification it cites requires,
  and its report carries the failing assertion.

Each reproducer is a standalone Cargo package: its `Cargo.toml` declares an empty
`[workspace]` table and depends on the affected crate through a relative `path`, and its
`src/main.rs` runs one scenario, so that running it exits non-zero on the affected commit.

## 6. Fixes

Under `fix`, every finding of the batch's objectives is patched:

- `unsafety`: the entry point is made safe;
- `contracts`: the `# Safety` obligation or `// SAFETY:` justification is corrected, or,
  when the contract can be broken, the code it guards, and the reproducer becomes a UB
  regression test;
- `ub`, `equiv` and `logic`: the defect is patched, and the reproducer becomes a
  regression test of the same kind, a UB test, an equivalence test or a unit test, on the
  side of the module it reaches. A UB
  regression test either runs without triggering a sanitizer, or fails to compile because
  the patch removed the safe path that reached the defect;
- `ergonomics`: the API is improved, and its consumers in the crate follow;
- `idiom`, `conventions` and `misc`: the transliteration, deviation or defect is fixed;
- `revisit`: every report that still reproduces is patched, as for its objective.

In a Crustify-generated batch, fixes follow the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md);
outside one, the repository's contributor instructions. Every test a review adds is classified as [`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)
describes and placed where the conventions place tests of its kind, or, outside a
Crustify-generated batch, in the reviewed crate's own suite for that kind.

## 7. Gates

The gates [`testing-gates`](../testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section gives a wave's
end run in its last review batch, which launches once every translation batch of the wave
has landed, and whose task's `wave_gates` says so: Miri in every wave. A module's end's,
every test under every available sanitizer and BSan over everything the module landed,
run in its module pass, when the wave is the module's last: no other translation wave in
`schedule.json` belongs to its module and runs after it. Each runs on the wave's tip
before any change, and again on the landed tree under `fix`. Without
`fix`, each true positive a gate finds is filed as a UB report. A BSan report on an earlier
wave's items belongs to the last wave's review.

## 8. Landing

A review batch lands two commits, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Landing section describes: first its
`crustify/reviews/` changes, so the reproducers run on the affected commit, then its
changes to the Rust tree, if any.

## 9. Plan corrections

A planner run that corrects what an earlier run decided files each correction as a finding
under `crustify/reviews/planner/`: `modules/` for `modules.json` and
`schedule.json`, and one sub-directory per tool artifact. Adding what the plan lacks,
updating it to the current schema, re-deriving entries under a rule that has changed and
re-planning the waves a change moves are no findings.

Each finding is its own `<slug>` directory, named for the finding
(`split-libavutil-hash`), never for the run, and never reused. Its `report.md` states:

- what the earlier plan decided, quoting the entries changed;
- the evidence against it: linker outputs, sources and tool queries, with the exact
  commands and paths to rerun them;
- the edit and what it moves downstream: modules, waves or batches, and the waves
  re-emitted; and
- any question only the user can answer.

workset adds; a workset that made no API item unsafe has none.

### 3.4 Equivalence (`equiv`)

Functional equivalence defects in the workset's API that its equivalence tests missed,
while the C it translates exists: in a port, until the module's switch. A divergence is a defect only when it is unintended: a doc comment, a `CHANGELOG`
entry, a named test asserting the new behaviour or a commit message explaining it marks it
deliberate, and one that corrects a C defect on purpose is no finding.

### 3.5 Logic (`logic`)

Behaviour that departs from the library's intended specification, in the workset's public
API or its private implementation, that its tests missed. The specification is, from the
most authoritative: the formats and standards the library implements, its documentation,
what its own test suites assert, and its maintainers' stated intent. A finding cites what
the behaviour departs from. Where the C departs from it too, the defect is not copied into
the Rust, and the finding records the C's. A leak, a deadlock or a panic on valid input
departs from nearly every specification.

### 3.6 Ergonomics (`ergonomics`)

Public API that is harder to use than it needs to be: its names, its conversions, its
iterators, builders or defaults where the C takes long argument lists, and the standard
traits its types lack. An item's safe API is fixed by the first batch that gives it one, a
wrap included, so its ergonomics are reviewed there.

### 3.7 Idiom (`idiom`)

Ported implementation that transliterates its C rather than using Rust's own means: index
loops where iterators fit, status codes where `Result` and `?` fit, lengths and releases
carried by hand where ownership carries them.

### 3.8 Conventions (`conventions`)

Deviations from the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md), in a Crustify-generated
batch only, unsafe code outside its regions included.

### 3.9 Misc (`misc`)

Any other defect in the workset.

### 3.10 Test adequacy (`test-adequacy`)

Gaps in the workset's tests: the C and Rust execution paths, and the states and
transitions, that the codebase's external and inline test suites leave unreached, found by
reading those suites against the code and measured as
[`testing-builds`](../testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section describes; assertions too
weak to fail when the code is wrong; tests outside the suite of their kind; and the C test
cases none carries over. A gap is filled with tests, not filed: the coverage measurement
shows the delta.

### 3.11 Revisit (`revisit`)

The reports an earlier review filed, each rerun through its reproducer on the current
tree. One that still reproduces stays a finding of its objective; one that no longer does
has its report updated with the commit that changed the verdict; one that was never a
defect is removed, with the reason in the commit message.

### 3.12 Disclosure (`disclose`)

A `disclosure.md` beside each report that the user can send to the affected project's
maintainers unchanged: under 450 words, following the project's conventions for
disclosing security and UB issues, in an email-friendly format naming the maintainers when
it goes by email first. It includes a small snippet and the sanitizer crash or failing
assertion, offers the reproducer on request, and offers patches only under `fix`. It ends
with: `Found by [Crustify](https://github.com/crustify-rs/crustify), an experimental
UB/soundness auditing agent developed at UC Berkeley and running on <model name>, then
manually reviewed and independently reproduced.`

### 3.13 Fix (`fix`)

Whether a review patches what it finds. Without it, a review changes nothing outside
its reviews dir but the tests that fill the gaps `test-adequacy` finds.

## 4. Reports

A review batch files its findings under its reviews dir, as
[`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Reviews section spells it,
each in its own `<slug>` directory, holding its report and, when it has one, its
reproducer, in the sub-directory of its objective:

| objective | sub-directory |
|---|---|
| `unsafety` | `unsafe/` |
| `contracts`, of a gateway | `contracts/ffi_export/` |
| `contracts`, of other unsafe code | `contracts/ffi_import/` |
| `ub`, on the safe interface | `ub_safe/` |
| `ub`, on the unsafe interface | `ub_unsafe/` |
| `ub`, through an export | `ub_export/` |
| `equiv` | `equiv/` |
| `logic` | `logic/` |
| `ergonomics` | `ergonomics/` |
| `idiom` | `idiom/` |
| `conventions` | `conventions/` |
| `misc` | `misc/` |

A tool may add sub-directories for findings on its own output. A defect in a tool
rather than in the reviewed codebase, Crustify included, is no finding: it is a proposal,
with its reproducer, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Proposals
section describes.

A report states what is wrong, where, the evidence that proves it, and, under `fix`, how
it was fixed. It carries everything needed to rerun its reproducer from a clean checkout:
the exact command and the sanitizer output or failing assertion it produced. Neither a
report nor a reproducer carries an API key, in a core dump or anywhere else: a reviews dir
may be published.

## 5. Reproducers

A `ub`, `equiv` or `logic` candidate becomes a finding only once a reproducer proves it,
and so does a `contracts` candidate that claims a contract can be broken. A contract that merely
asks for more than the implementation needs, or a missing justification, is a finding
without one.

- A UB reproducer triggers one of the available sanitizers from Rust, and its report
  carries the sanitizer's trace. One targeting the safe public API carries
  `#[forbid(unsafe_code)]`; one targeting the unsafe API, or breaking a contract, honours
  the `# Safety` obligation. One reaching an export calls it as C would, through its raw
  binding, within the C declaration's contract.
- An equivalence reproducer fails one of [`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s equivalence
  comparisons while running the raw C and the public Rust API, and its report carries the
  failing assertion. Once the C is gone, a behaviour finding is a `logic` one.
- A logic reproducer fails a Rust assertion of what the specification it cites requires,
  and its report carries the failing assertion.

Each reproducer is a standalone Cargo package: its `Cargo.toml` declares an empty
`[workspace]` table and depends on the affected crate through a relative `path`, and its
`src/main.rs` runs one scenario, so that running it exits non-zero on the affected commit.

## 6. Fixes

Under `fix`, every finding of the batch's objectives is patched:

- `unsafety`: the entry point is made safe;
- `contracts`: the `# Safety` obligation or `// SAFETY:` justification is corrected, or,
  when the contract can be broken, the code it guards, and the reproducer becomes a UB
  regression test;
- `ub`, `equiv` and `logic`: the defect is patched, and the reproducer becomes a
  regression test of the same kind, a UB test, an equivalence test or a unit test, on the
  side of the module it reaches. A UB
  regression test either runs without triggering a sanitizer, or fails to compile because
  the patch removed the safe path that reached the defect;
- `ergonomics`: the API is improved, and its consumers in the crate follow;
- `idiom`, `conventions` and `misc`: the transliteration, deviation or defect is fixed;
- `revisit`: every report that still reproduces is patched, as for its objective.

In a Crustify-generated batch, fixes follow the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md);
outside one, the repository's contributor instructions. Every test a review adds is classified as [`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)
describes and placed where the conventions place tests of its kind, or, outside a
Crustify-generated batch, in the reviewed crate's own suite for that kind.

## 7. Gates

The gates [`testing-gates`](../testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section gives a wave's
end run in its last review batch, which launches once every translation batch of the wave
has landed, and whose task's `wave_gates` says so: Miri in every wave. A module's end's,
every test under every available sanitizer and BSan over everything the module landed,
run in its module pass, when the wave is the module's last: no other translation wave in
`schedule.json` belongs to its module and runs after it. Each runs on the wave's tip
before any change, and again on the landed tree under `fix`. Without
`fix`, each true positive a gate finds is filed as a UB report. A BSan report on an earlier
wave's items belongs to the last wave's review.

## 8. Landing

A review batch lands two commits, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Landing section describes: first its
`crustify/reviews/` changes, so the reproducers run on the affected commit, then its
changes to the Rust tree, if any.

## 9. Plan corrections

A planner run that corrects what an earlier run decided files each correction as a finding
under `crustify/reviews/planner/`: `modules/` for `modules.json` and
`schedule.json`, and one sub-directory per tool artifact. Adding what the plan lacks,
updating it to the current schema, re-deriving entries under a rule that has changed and
re-planning the waves a change moves are no findings.

Each finding is its own `<slug>` directory, named for the finding
(`split-libavutil-hash`), never for the run, and never reused. Its `report.md` states:

- what the earlier plan decided, quoting the entries changed;
- the evidence against it: linker outputs, sources and tool queries, with the exact
  commands and paths to rerun them;
- the edit and what it moves downstream: modules, waves or batches, and the waves
  re-emitted; and
- any question only the user can answer.

# Mandatory questions

   now or we can brainstorm them during the live session. You can also let the

   - Answer: what the parent campaigns consume from libc, the entities their dependency

     `crustify-rs/libgit2-bindings`, 871 functions, 95 structs and 2 globals, counted per
     module over its 168 modules that use libc; growing as the parents' waves need more

4. **Which model and billing should do the translation work?**
   (`id: translate-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5`, the parent
     `libgit2-crustify`'s answer since 2026-11-13, in the current template's format:
     `<claude | codex>, <subscription | api>[, proxy: openrouter][, args: ...]`
   - Format: `<provider/model, api | subscription>`, e.g.
     `openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5, api`. The provider is the first
     segment and selects both the billing rate table and the backend CLI.
     Supported providers:
     - `anthropic/<model>` — Anthropic direct, driven by Claude Code;
     - `openai/<model>` — OpenAI direct, driven by Codex;
     - `openrouter/<vendor>/<model>` — OpenRouter, which resells every vendor
       behind one key, so the vendor segment picks the CLI: `anthropic/*` is
       driven by Claude Code and everything else by Codex. OpenRouter
       supports `api` billing only.

5. **Do you want agentic review after translated work lands? If so, which
   model and billing should perform each review?** (`id: review-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5`, after each wave

6. **Should I run fully autonomously end to end?** (`id: autonomy`)
   - Answer: `no`

Unanswered optional questions use their defaults.

7. **Which model and billing should plan the campaign, and how many planner runs
   should it make? Each run emits what the plan lacks and corrects what the runs
   before it committed.** (`id: plan-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5, runs: 1` for an

8. **Should the campaign use the default batching and parallelism settings, or
   customize them?** (`id: workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`, the parent's answer.

9. **What batch caps should review agents use? We recommend the same caps as
   translation by default.** (`id: review-workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`, the parent's answer.

10. **Which objectives should review agents review for? By default, every one the
    reviewer offers.** (`id: review-objectives`)
    - Answer: `all`
    - Without `fix`, reviewers report and reproduce what they find but patch nothing.

11. **Which sanitizers should the campaign build and test under? By default, every one

    - Answer: `asan-ubsan, tsan, bsan`, instrumenting the Rust; the system's glibc they
      link is not instrumented. MSan is not built.
    - From 2026-11-13, as in the parent: BSan runs over the whole workspace, and as a
      regression gate, only once before each ship point; otherwise an agent may run it on
      small things, the tests its own work adds or changes and a review's reproducer,
      each test named and under a `timeout`. This departs from the `testing-gates`
      skill's Regressions section.
    - Miri needs no build and is always on.

    enabled or disabled?** (`id: target-config`)

      the host link, so glibc is not built; `c/` is its source, for reading its behaviour,

    component), the parent `libgit2-crustify`'s answer: a side campaign's settings are its
    parent's.
- **At which points should the wrapper ship?** (`id: ship`)
  - Answer: with the parent: the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins when the parent
    ships, each with the user's approval.

## Commits

13. **Which git identity should the campaign's commits carry: an author, and any
    co-authors? By default, Crustify's own, `crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the
    GitHub account `crustify-ai`), as the author, with no co-author.** (`id: identity`)
    - Answer: `author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>, co-authors: crustify
      <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the GitHub account `crustify-ai`)

## Autonomy (if question 6 is answered `no`)

Answer these approval-gate questions only if question 6 is answered `no`.

    - Answer: `no`

    (`id: gates.translation`)
    - Answer: `no`, the parent's answer
16. **Should I wait for your approval between modules?** (`id: gates.module`)
    - Answer: `no`

    - Answer: `no`

# Benchmark recording questions

    - Answer: `<repo-checkout>/crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md`, `standard` template

# Additional instructions

Unless otherwise stated, preserve the format of the dashboard exactly.

commit d79690087aba0d091dcf1ef9122ed5fe545bbe2b
Author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>
Date:   Fri Nov 13 22:24:20 2026 +0000

    iofwrite.c: wrap 1 item (wave-5/batch-0/run-1)
    
    fn::fwrite
    
    fwrite is bound as FileRef::write_all(&self, &[u8]) -> io::Result<()>:
    fwrite(bytes, 1, len, stream) between flockfile and funlockfile,
    whatever the stream's locking mode, so the bytes land in the stream's
    buffer as they are, NUL and invalid UTF-8 included. It is the write the
    parent's FileWriter makes, one call per io::Write::write. A short count
    is fwrite's failure and fails the call, as fprintf's does: after a
    failed flush the stream has discarded its buffer, so a retry of the
    rest would write on as if nothing failed. Ok is therefore the whole
    slice, and carries no count.
    
    fwrite returns its full count when a line-buffered stream's flush of a
    line that fits its buffer fails, where fprintf fails. The binding reads
    the stream's error indicator with ferror before and after the call,
    under the same hold of the lock, and fails when it goes from clear to
    set. An indicator an earlier failure left set hides that one case, as
    its doc says. A wide stream fails with Other, no errno; an empty slice
    succeeds without touching the stream, as fwrite of no bytes does.
    
    The lock moved to File's home: FileRef::lock checks has_lock and takes
    flockfile, and its StreamLock releases with funlockfile on drop,
    unwinding included. print takes it too, and fprintf.rs loses its own
    copies; its tests pass unchanged. The raw bindings gain fwrite, and
    setvbuf, clearerr and _IOLBF for the tests.
    
    Tests: 10 equivalence tests against the raw fwrite and against
    fprintf(stream, "%s", text) on growing, file, line-buffered,
    by-caller-locked, read-only, full, failing and wide streams; 17 unit
    tests and 3 inline. Plain and under ASan, the stream suites under TSan,
    two named tests under BSan, each new test alone under Miri (the 27 that
    call C stop at their first foreign call). Rust coverage over src/:
    144 of 144 lines. ffimap api diff: fn::fwrite new, the rest kept.
    
    Proposal filed: sticky-error-state (made on crustify's
    libgit2-crustify/evolution/sticky-error-state, 57fd7a3, for review).
    Lesson: a test of a failing stream reads it only after its last write.

  waves 0 to 4 are done.

- fwrite takes a pointer and a count, which binding-symbols' Buffers rule
  makes one slice. The binding writes &[u8] exactly, NUL bytes included,
  with no CString, and returns the bytes written, a short count on

- fprintf's "%s" over a &CStr is bound already, so no item would be
  planned (an item landed with its objective is not scheduled again).

- 1 csu/errno-loc.c, frozen: __errno_location, with stdlib/errno.h's
  declaration and errno macro (787a802). csu/ is the TU Linux compiles
  (sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/Makefile, subdir csu); nptl/errno-loc.c only
  includes it.
